source.title: (S)GD over Diagonal Linear Networks: Implicit Regularisation, Large Stepsizes and Edge of Stability
source.authors: Mathieu Even; Scott Pesme; Suriya Gunasekar; Nicolas Flammarion

record.file_problem: The full text is present. Some figures are flattened, so their plotted values cannot be recovered.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports how optimizer and stepsize affect test loss and sparse recovery in synthetic noiseless regression with diagonal linear networks, extending the claim's generalization subject to a different setting.
record.gate_note: The study does not test fitting random labels or generalization on natural labels. Its test-loss and recovery results concern sparse regression against a sparse ground-truth predictor, not the listed claim versions. Figure-only values are recorded as such. Cited findings from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study reports original results on stepsize, stochasticity and sparse recovery in diagonal linear regression networks, but tests none of V1–V8. Its batch comparisons run to convergence rather than holding epochs fixed (V5), and its raw Hessian measures do not test magnitude-aware sharpness or rankings of generalization gaps (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors prove convergence under stepsize assumptions and characterize the resulting interpolator through a trajectory-dependent implicit regularization problem. Larger stepsizes improve SGD sparse recovery but can hinder GD on centered data; uncentered data can change GD's behavior. Their edge-of-stability explanation is partly heuristic.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses two-layer diagonal linear networks on noiseless synthetic sparse regression and measures test loss or distance to a sparse interpolator; it does not use natural-label classification or random-label memorization.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer, stepsize, minibatch size, and whether the Gaussian inputs are centered. The text also reports different Hessian flatness trends by optimizer and metric.

fits_no_version.finding: For centered Gaussian sparse regression, increasing stepsize improves SGD's final predictor recovery but worsens GD's recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stepsize can have opposite effects on generalization for single-example SGD and full-batch GD in diagonal linear networks trained to convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gaussian inputs with mean 5 in every coordinate, larger stepsizes help sparse recovery and GD and SGD behave similarly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of large stepsizes on sparse recovery depends on input centering and the orientation of the input mean relative to the sparse predictor.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing stepsize lowers GD's maximum Hessian eigenvalue despite worse recovery, while lowering SGD's Hessian trace alongside better recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Raw Hessian flatness measures can give different accounts of generalization depending on the optimizer and curvature statistic.

record.problems: The experiments use small synthetic sparse-regression settings, not natural-label classification. Several result values are available only in figures whose numbers cannot be recovered from the supplied text. The authors describe some edge-of-stability discussion as heuristic rather than formal.
record.rows_left_out: No further rows were retained. Figure 2 and Figure 3 primarily report gain-vector geometry, trajectories, and loss behavior without a separately stated held-out test result beyond the outcomes represented by R1–R2. Appendix Figure 6 reports sparse recovery for SGD at the edge of stability but does not provide a held-out generalization measure.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; mentioning scalar adaptive stepsizes in a theorem does not test this comparison.
Large-batch held-out penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their removal through recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness tracking generalization gaps and outperforming norm- or margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are assessed against the listed claim versions; cannot_determine for these unlinked rows does not deny the qualitative effects explicitly reported in the text. Related sparse-regression and raw-curvature findings do not justify version verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Large-batch generalization gaps under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a measure tracking the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

tranche.reason: The study examines stepsize-dependent implicit bias and sparse recovery in diagonal linear regression networks. It tests none of V1–V8: its batch comparisons concern converged solutions rather than fixed epoch budgets, and its Hessian measures do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or rank generalization gaps.

source_check.notes: Figures 1 and 4 report squared predictor distance to the minimum ℓ1 interpolator; exact plotted outcomes are not stated numerically. The qualitative findings and authors-conclusion paraphrase are supported.
